Pickers drawn over details, dialogs, radios and a scroller

Five more controls from ui-feed.dev, rebuilt with HTML-in-canvas: a drop-down, popovers, a segmented control, a row of letter boxes and a carousel. The browser already has an element for most of these, and several of them paint in the top layer, where a canvas can't draw them. I wanted to know which native elements could stand in and still be drawn, and if a scroller that the canvas draws would still scroll and snap by itself.

Credit: every control on this page is a rebuild of a demo on ui-feed.dev, and each section links to the original it came from. The originals are far higher fidelity than these, so go and look at them. These are examples of what HTML-in-canvas makes possible with a native element underneath, not replacements. I worked from the published demos rather than their source: I looked at what each one does, worked out the mechanism and built it again. The designs and the ideas are theirs.

Shoe size

The picker of a <select> is painted in the top layer, so a canvas has no picture of it. This drop-down is a <details> with a radio for each size. The summary is the box that shows the size, the radios give the arrow keys and the sold-out size is a disabled radio. The canvas draws the list sliding open and turns the chevron over. A tap on a size closes the list, and an arrow key doesn't. The shoe grows a little with the size.

Bicycle parts

Each dot is a <button> and each card is a <dialog> that is opened without showModal(), so it stays out of the top layer and has a picture. The card holds a <form method="dialog">, and its button adds the part or takes it off again. The canvas draws the card growing out of its dot, the pointer under it, and the plus turning into a cross. Escape or a tap on the wall closes the card.

Glaze

Four radios in one group. The canvas draws the bar, a thumb that slides to the checked radio in the colour of its glaze, and the names twice: once light, and once through the thumb in a colour that shows on it. The mug is drawn once for each glaze on a plain canvas, always the same shape, and the new glaze is wiped over the old one from the right. The line of text is an <output>.

Crossword

One <input type="text"> lies across the pink row, with a maxlength of seven. It is drawn with no alpha, so it takes the tap, the keyboard and the caret but none of its own text shows. The canvas reads its value and stamps each letter into a square, and draws a caret in the square where the field's caret is. The grid is a <table> written from the rows in the markup, and the clue is a heading.

Tulips

The slides are in a <div> that scrolls sideways with scroll-snap-type. The canvas draws that element at whatever position it has scrolled to, so a swipe, a wheel and the arrow keys are the browser's own, and so is the snap. The tulips are drawn by the canvas on top, a little faster than the slides. The lines at the bottom are radios: choosing one scrolls the element, and where the element comes to rest checks a radio.

How it works

Each control is a custom element on the same base class as the trees and timelines. Its shadow root holds a canvas with content="drawable", and the native elements are children of that canvas.

A canvas can only draw an element that is laid out inside it. The picker of a <select>, a popover and a modal <dialog> are all painted in the top layer, outside the canvas, so none of them has a picture to draw. The first two controls use elements that stay in the canvas: a <details> with radios for the drop-down, and a <dialog> with the open attribute for each card.

Closing is the same trick each time. A closed <details> and a closed <dialog> have nothing to draw, so the control cancels the event that would close the element, draws it shut over a fifth of a second and then closes it.

The carousel needs no scroll code for touch. The scroller is a drawable child, the browser scrolls it and raises a paint event at each step, and the control reads scrollLeft in its paint handler to place the tulips and the bright marker.

Live checks

Findings

  • A <details> with radios can be drawn as a drop-down, and a <select> can't. The picker of a select is in the top layer and has no picture. The stand-in keeps the arrow keys, the disabled option and the form value. It loses the phone's own picker and typing a letter to jump to an option, and a screen reader is told about a group of radios where the original has a list box.
  • A <dialog> with the open attribute is drawn like any other child. It isn't modal, so it stays in the canvas. Its <form method="dialog"> would close it at once, so the control cancels the submit, draws the card shut and then calls close() with the button's value. The dialog ended with returnValue "add".
  • For one frame after an element closes, its box is short and its picture is still the open one. Drawn at the new size, the whole list was squashed into the summary. I saw it in a screenshot, not in a check. The control draws that frame at the height the element had.
  • The element drawn last answers the tap. With each name drawn after its radio, the point on a segment answered the <label>. That still checks the radio, but the radios are now drawn last, with no alpha.
  • A scroll-snap element drawn by the canvas scrolls and snaps by itself. A click on the third marker scrolled it 720 units with 45 paint events on the way, and nothing in the control listens for those to draw. Left at 980 units by a script, it snapped to 1080 and the control checked the fourth radio. A swipe by touch in the emulated phone moved one slide, and a vertical swipe on the slides scrolled the page.
  • A text field drawn with no alpha still takes the tap, the focus and the typing. Its own caret is transparent, because a caret that blinks in a picture nobody sees still raises paints. The canvas draws a caret from selectionStart and asks for a paint twice a second while the field has focus.
  • The pictures are far from the originals. Their shoe, bicycle, mug and tulips are photographs. Mine are paths and gradients on a plain canvas.
  • Not verified: everything on a phone. In particular the on-screen keyboard over the crossword (capitals, word suggestions, an IME), a fling on the carousel, and what a screen reader says about each control.
